In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two species studied differed in their response to cutting in terms of nodule and root shedding.
fine roots and nodules are lost following cutting, but that this is not a serious problem in either of these species.
the extent of nodule and root shedding is not related to stem regrowth rate or to the root:leaf ratio, and that the factors controlling the shedding are different for nodules and roots.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fine roots of both species and the nodules of Sesbania are sensitive to coppicing, but the sensitivity of nodules in both species and of the roots in Leucaenas may be less than that reported for other species.

cutting has a significant impact on the nodule biomass of Sesbanias, and that the extent of the impact is related to the species' allocation to root and nodule tissue, but the effects of cutting are not as great for Sesbanias as has been reported for other legume tree species.

the fine roots and nodules of both species were relatively insensitive to cutting, but that the greater below-ground biomass allocation of Leucaena may be the basis for its relatively greater resistance to cutting.
The main takeaway from our work is that

nodule biomass decreases more rapidly and more dramatically than fine root biomass in response to cutting, and this difference may be related to differences in allocation to below-ground biomass and to the greater sensitivity of nodule than root biomass to cutting.
the root:shoot ratio of a tree is not a reliable indicator of its sensitivity to cutting, because the roots are only one of many below-ground storage tissues.
the fine roots of Sesbania and Leucaene are not sensitive to coppicing.
